Article Title: 'Served nation with dedication': PM Modi, Rahul Gandhi pay tribute to Manmohan Singh on birth anniversary
Article Text:
Tributes pour in for former PM Manmohan Singh on his birth anniversary.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday paid tribute to former prime minister Manmohan Singh on his birth anniversary, remembering his long public life and service to the nation."Tributes to our former prime minister Dr Manmohan Singh Ji on his birth anniversary. He spent many years in public life and served the nation with dedication," PM Modi said in a post on X.Congress Parliamentary Party (CPP) chairperson Sonia Gandhi and leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi also paid floral tributes to the former prime minister on his birth anniversary.Sharing a post on X, Rahul Gandhi said, "On the birth anniversary of former Prime Minister Dr Manmohan Singh ji, I pay my humble respects to him. With his humility, integrity, and foresight, he gave a new direction to the country's economy and social justice. His historic decisions and invaluable contributions to the making of India will forever continue to guide us."Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra also paid tribute to Singh saying, "I offer my humble respects. As a skilled economist and successful politician, Dr Manmohan Singh ji imparted extraordinary momentum to India's development and elevated the nation's prosperity to new heights.""Through his visionary and inclusive economic policies, he enriched every section of society.Dr Manmohan Singh ji's unprecedented contributions to the country's development will always be remembered. I pay homage to his memories," he added.Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge also remembered the former prime minister, saying, "We remember with profound respect the extraordinary contribution of former Prime Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh to India’s nation-building. A visionary statesman, his landmark economic reforms transformed India’s growth trajectory, created new opportunities and helped lift millions out of poverty. His humility, integrity and wisdom defined his public life. ""He led with quiet dignity and compassion, placing inclusive growth and the welfare of the most vulnerable at the heart of governance. The rights-based framework of his government remains an enduring testament to this vision. On his birth anniversary, we pay our heartfelt homage to a statesman whose legacy of honest public service, inclusive development and transformative reforms will continue to inspire generations," he added.Manmohan Singh was born on September 26, 1932, in Gah, in present-day Pakistan, then part of undivided India. He died in New Delhi on December 26, 2024.Singh became India's 14th prime minister on May 22, 2004, and returned for a second consecutive term on May 22, 2009. He served as prime minister until 2014.Before becoming prime minister, Singh served as Union finance minister from 1991 to 1996. During his tenure, India introduced a wide-ranging programme of economic reforms that reshaped the country's economy and earned international recognition.Singh's public life spanned several decades, during which he held key positions in government and played a significant role in shaping India's economic policy.
Article Summary: Tributes pour in for former pm manmohan singh on his birth anniversary. Pm modi: he spent many years in public life and served the nation with dedication. Rahul gandhi: with his humility, integrity, and foresight, he gave a new direction to the country's economy.

Article Title: 'No hard feelings': US on India's stern warning over Russia Sanctions Act
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: The United States on Saturday said that it was looking to meet India's massive energy needs, days after US President Donald Trump signed the 'Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026', which authorises him to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries buying Russian oil and gas."We are looking to also become a huge source of India's energy needs. We're increasing our hydrocarbon exports,” a senior US state department official told news agency PTI.“The demands are great, and the needs for oil are there. We are looking for alternatives. But I would say before even the war, India had been looking to diversify when it came to energy for a long time. It's not a new concept. We just need to expedite it faster,” he added.The US official also played down New Delhi's warning over the contentious law and said that India's response was expected after the US Congress took a pretty hard approach, especially publicly.“India has been looking for a long time to diversify its energy sources. They're a country that has massive energy needs,” the official told PTI.“You had members of Congress calling out India in particular, so of course India has to respond.We understand that. They have a domestic constituency, as do we. Like, there are no sort of hard feelings on any of that kind of activity," he added.Last week, the ministry of external affairs warned the US of the legislation’s potential impact on the US-India relationship.“This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side,” the ministry said.The official said that the new act gave President Trump a new tool in his toolbox.“That doesn't necessarily mean he deploys it tomorrow, but he has the opportunity to. His focus is on ending this war. It's been something he campaigned on and something he's been dedicated to from the beginning,” he said.“We're looking for our friends, especially like India, to help support that effort. But I think you'll have to stay tuned on how the bill gets implemented. But there is a broad national security waiver, so you can imagine also the president, there's a scenario, the president uses that as well,” he added."Now, with President Trump's incredibly successful operation in Venezuela, we are moving into a better position that countries like India are going to be able to get access to that market,” he added.
Article Summary: U.s. looking to become a huge source of india's energy needs, official says. Us president donald trump signed the 'lindsey o graham sanctioning russia and iran act of 2026' new delhi warned the us of the legislation’s potential impact on the us-india relationship.

Article Title: A day after Wangchuk compares Ladakh situation with Tibet; Central Tibetan Administration calls comparison misplaced, inaccurate
Article Text:
Sonam Wangchuk

SRINAGAR: A day after Leh Apex Body (LAB) member and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk compared situation in Ladakh with Tibet , the Central Tibetan Administration, based in Dharamshala, Friday evening expressed deep concern over remarks of Wangchuk called the comparison misplaced and inaccurate and stating “Tibet continues to remain under China's authoritarian rule. ”“The Central Tibetan Administration expresses deep concern over remarks made by Sonam Wangchuk in his recent public speech in Ladakh, in which he compared the situation in Ladakh with that of inside Tibet,” Tenzin Lekshay official spokesperson of the Central Tibetan Administration said, adding that CTA considers such a comparison misplaced and inaccurate.“His statement doesn't reflect the real situation inside Tibet. Tibet continues to remain under China's authoritarian rule. where Tibetans face systematic repression of their fundamental rights, religious freedom; and intensification of measures aimed at erasing its distinct cultural identity,” Lekshay added.Wangchuk, addressing people in Leh on the first anniversary of the Sept 24, 2025 violence, said the alleged breach of promises made to Ladakh over the Sixth Schedule and statehood was the “root cause” of last year’s protests.On September 24 2025, police allegedly opened fire on protesters demanding Sixth Schedule status and statehood for Ladakh after demonstrations turned violent, killing four people and injuring nearly 90.He feared he could be subjected to an “encounter” for speaking out against what he called atrocities in Ladakh, a year after police firing killed four protesters in Leh. Drawing a comparison with Tibet, Wangchuk said Ladakhis had chosen India because of its democracy.“Today, such atrocities are being committed in Ladakh that even China is not doing in Tibet. That is what you are seeing today,” he said.He sought a people’s tribunal to probe the killings, saying a judicial commission set up by Union home ministry had yet to submit its report. “Last year on this day, four people died... Bullets hit their chests, backs, and heads. Those were not pellets that would merely injure you or hurt your eyes. Bullets were fired indiscriminately from automatic weapons, like AK-47s, at the unarmed youth of Ladakh who were peacefully demanding their rights,” Wangchuk alleged. He rejected claims that the protests were triggered by him. He alleged that before the 2020 LAHDC-Leh elections, Ladakhi representatives opposed to holding polls were taken to New Delhi on a special flight and promised statehood and Sixth Schedule status.He blamed “govt failure to honour those promises” for last year’s demonstrations. Authorities imposed curfew-like restrictions in Leh after the alleged “arson and rioting” and subsequent police firing last year. FIRs were filed and 81 people arrested, including Wangchuk. He was charged under NSA and sent to Jodhpur jail. After 170 days, Union govt withdrew his detention on March 14 this year and he was set free.He feared further action, saying: “They sent me to jail. Inquiries have been made against me. Only an encounter is left. I am ready for that. It is my last wish. Experts tell me that you will be subjected to an encounter. So be it. Let the country wake up, this is my hope.”A complete shutdown was observed in Leh on Thursday, designated as Martyr’s Day. Wangchuk accused authorities of stopping people from attending the rally, a claim denied by police.Police said the Ladakh Buddhist Association had sought permission for a public meeting at Leh’s NDS stadium, which has a capacity of 10,000. The administration granted permission for a prayer meet from 10am to noon. Police claimed a turnout of 800 at the event and denied allegations that they erected barricades to stop people from reaching the venue.
Article Summary: Sonam wangchuk compared situation in ladakh with tibet. The central tibetan administration, based in dharamshala, called the comparison misplaced and inaccurate. Wangchuk said the alleged breach of promises made to ladakh over the sixth schedule and statehood was the ‘root cause’ of last year’s protests.

NEW DELHI: Jantar Mantar in Delhi was heavily barricaded on Friday following nationwide protests demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Visuals from the protest site showed multiple layers of barricades, forming a clear cordon around Jantar Mantar. Buses have been used to block the entrances and there is heavy police deployment.The Indian Youth Congress was scheduled to march from Raisina Road to Jantar Mantar.CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke said on Friday that his organisation would launch nationwide protests from October 2 if Kumar did not resign by Saturday. Police had put up barricades near Rajiv Bhawan. The protesting leaders, including Gogoi, attempted to cross them and were subsequently detained.Those detained included AICC secretary Manoj Chauhan, Seva Dal president Deep Bayan and APCC general secretary Udit Bhanu Das, along with several others.Congress spokesperson Bedabrata Bora alleged that the leaders were "forcefully arrested" and claimed that "this is yet another threat to democracy".The developments comes a day after leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi criticised Kumar following reports of differences within the Election Commission over the SIR of electoral rolls.

Article Title: Unease within NDA over EC-SIR row? Three BJP allies seek poll body clarification as opposition keeps up pressure

NEW DELHI: Unease within the ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA) over a media report concerning Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar surfaced on Friday, with three BJP allies urging the Election Commission of India (ECI) to issue a clearer response.Union minister and Lok Janshakti Party (LJP) president Chirag Paswan was the first NDA ally to urge the ECI to dispel “misgivings in the minds of the people.”“Let me make it clear that, as part of the government, I do not intend to defend what is a constitutional body. I am also not much worried about the allegations made by the opposition, which will always take a stand that suits it politically,” Paswan told reporters in Patna.“However, if people start losing trust in the electoral system, that will not augur well for democracy. Therefore, I think the Election Commission must come out with its clarification more forcefully. It need not respond to what Rahul Gandhi and his associates are saying, but it must dispel misgivings in the minds of the people,” the Hajipur MP added.Rashtriya Lok Morcha (RLM) chief and Rajya Sabha MP Upendra Kushwaha also called for a clarification, saying the controversy had created “confusion” among the public."The controversy regarding the SIR has created a situation of significant confusion among the public. The matter needs to be addressed. The Election Commission should immediately issue a clarification regarding the actual situation to clear up this confusion," Kushwaha posted on X.The Telugu Desam Party (TDP) described the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise in Andhra Pradesh as a “success,” while noting that a clarification from the ECI would be “beneficial”.“The exercise has been a success. Even the opposition has not been able to substantiate its concerns regarding the process in Andhra Pradesh. At the same time, the Election Commission of India is a constitutional institution entrusted with a crucial responsibility in our democracy. Therefore, whenever questions are raised by anyone, providing appropriate clarification and maintaining transparency will only help strengthen public confidence in the institution,” TDP MP Lavu Srikrishna Devarayalu said.The allies’ remarks came after a report in The Indian Express said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had, on at least 14 occasions over the past 10 months, recorded objections to decisions and orders apparently issued without their knowledge or recommendation.The objections reportedly related to changes to the statutory voter registration Form 6, the process for adding and deleting names from electoral rolls, and the centralised control of the electoral roll database.The report prompted opposition parties to demand the CEC’s removal and call for the SIR exercise to be halted.The ECI, however, asserted that differences of opinion among its members were a “normal part of deliberation” and maintained that its final decisions, including those concerning the SIR, had been “unanimous”.According to the Commission, all its official orders and directions had legal sanction, while describing the suggestions made by the two Election Commissioners as efforts to improve electoral processes. Neither Sandhu nor Joshi has publicly commented on the objections attributed to them.The BJP, meanwhile, has played down the reported differences within the Commission, saying that the exchange of views during official deliberations reflected “pure democracy." The saffron party's West Bengal unit chief, Samik Bhattacharya, for instance, suggested that Gyanesh Kumar be awarded the Padma Bhushan, the country's third-highest civilan honour."The fact is, even the Congress party itself doesn't heed Rahul Gandhi's words; they don't take him seriously... Gyanesh Kumar deserves, at the very least, the Padma Bhushan... In a border state like this (West Bengal), Gyanesh Kumar took the initiative to remove the names of Bangladeshi infiltrators from the voter list," Bhattacharya said.Kumar, who became an Election Commissioner in 2024 and CEC in 2025, has repeatedly faced allegations from the Opposition that he has “favoured” the BJP.

Article Title: 'Compromised PM does it again': Congress targets Centre over bail for US national Matthew Aaron VanDyke held in terror conspiracy case

NEW DELHI: The release of US national Matthew Aaron VanDyke, who was arrested by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) in March in a case involving an alleged terror conspiracy linked to Myanmar-based ethnic armed groups, has triggered a political row, with the Congress questioning the circumstances of his release and alleging that US diplomatic pressure influenced the outcome."Our compromised PM has does it again. The PM has failed to protect India’s elections, institutions and our national security," Congress said in a post on X.VanDyke and six Ukrainian nationals were arrested by the NIA on March 13. According to the agency's allegations, the accused had entered India and travelled to restricted areas in the Northeast before crossing into Myanmar, where they allegedly came into contact with ethnic armed organisations and were involved in drone-warfare training. The NIA had initially registered the case under provisions of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA).The agency's March court submissions alleged that the accused supported anti-India insurgent groups. The NIA later told a Delhi court that the seven foreign nationals were allegedly linked to a drone attack on a civilian aircraft in Myanmar, although the investigation remained underway.The case took a fresh turn on September 8, when the NIA filed a chargesheet against the seven under Sections 21 and 23 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, without invoking UAPA provisions in the chargesheet.The agency said the UAPA investigation had not been closed and that a supplementary chargesheet could be filed if further offences were established.A Delhi court subsequently granted VanDyke default bail, observing that the chargesheet was "piecemeal" while the investigation into the UAPA offences remained pending. The 180-day statutory period for completing the investigation had also elapsed.On September 24, the court allowed VanDyke and the six Ukrainian nationals to travel to their respective countries for a month, subject to conditions. The court also released their passports.Congress has alleged that the development followed US pressure and questioned whether diplomatic intervention played a role. The party has also raised questions over how the foreign nationals obtained Indian visas and were able to travel to restricted areas of the Northeast before allegedly crossing into Myanmar.The government has maintained that the terror investigation against VanDyke and the other accused remains open.
Article Summary: Us national matthew aaron vandyke was arrested by the nia in a case involving an alleged terror conspiracy linked to myanmar-based ethnic armed groups. The congress has questioned the circumstances of his release and alleges that us diplomatic pressure influenced the outcome.

Article Title: The Backstory: When 'Tau' Devi Lal won the PM race, and then gave it away with a twist
Article Text:
Chaudhary Devi Lal, the former Haryana chief minister and deputy prime minister, who turned down the Prime Minister's post in 1989 in favour of VP Singh.

The Central Hall manoeuvre

The OG 'Tau'

From Haryana's farmer leader to national kingmaker

The shifting dynamics

Legacy that became a political dynasty

NEW DELHI: On December 1, 1989, the newly elected Janata Dal parliamentary party gathered in Parliament's Central Hall to decide who would lead the government that was about to replace Rajiv Gandhi's Congress. The leadership contest had already become a tug-of-war between VP Singh and Chandra Shekhar, with neither side willing to concede the top job.Then came an extraordinary political manoeuvre.VP Singh proposed Chaudhary Devi Lal's name. Chandra Shekhar seconded it. Devi Lal was declared elected as leader of the Janata Dal parliamentary party. And then the 75-year-old Haryana veteran stood up and proposed VP Singh for the Prime Minister post.Within minutes, the man who had just been chosen to lead the government had handed the job to someone else.VP Singh was elected leader and would become India's seventh Prime Minister. Devi Lal became deputy Prime Minister.The episode, one of the more remarkable leadership reversals in political history, has been recounted in several accounts of the 1989 transition. But this story is about Chaudhary Devi Lal, a man whose influence was built far from Delhi's power corridors and whose appeal rested heavily on Haryana's farmers and rural voters.The drama of December 1 was the culmination of days of uncertainty following the 1989 Lok Sabha election, which had ended Rajiv Gandhi's five-year tenure and produced a fractured mandate.The National Front, led by the Janata Dal, was in a position to form the government with outside support from the BJP and the Left parties. But before the government could be formed, the Janata Dal had to settle its own leadership question.VP Singh was the obvious national face of the anti-Congress campaign, having broken with Rajiv Gandhi and built his reputation around allegations of corruption in the previous government. Chandra Shekhar, meanwhile, had his own ambitions and was deeply reluctant to accept Singh as the party's leader.Devi Lal sat at the centre of the equation.A detailed account of the episode in journalist Neerja Chowdhury's 'How Prime Ministers Decide' describes a political formula worked out at Odisha Bhavan shortly before the parliamentary party meeting. The plan was simple but dramatic: Singh would propose Devi Lal's name, Devi Lal would then withdraw and propose Singh, and Chandra Shekhar would be persuaded to second Devi Lal's nomination.Chandra Shekhar agreed to second Devi Lal's name after being told that Devi Lal would be the candidate. He did not, however, know the full plan.When the meeting began in Central Hall, the arrangement played out almost exactly as planned. Singh proposed Devi Lal. Chandra Shekhar seconded him. But after Devi Lal's nomination, the Haryana leader proposed Singh instead. The assembled parliamentarians broke into applause and Singh was declared leader of the Janata Dal Parliamentary Party.Chandra Shekhar was furious.According to the account, he believed he had been assured that Devi Lal would become Prime Minister. After the meeting, he reportedly warned that the episode would have consequences for the future.That warning proved prescient. Less than a year later, Chandra Shekhar and Devi Lal would join forces against VP Singh, helping bring down the government they had helped create.Born on September 25, 1914, in what was then Punjab, Devi Lal entered politics through the freedom movement and went on to become one of Haryana's most influential leaders.He served as Haryana chief minister twice, from 1977 to 1979 and again from 1987 to 1989, before becoming deputy Prime Minister at the Centre.His political persona was very different from that of the Delhi establishment. Devi Lal cultivated the image of a rustic, accessible farmer leader and became popularly known as 'Tau', or elder uncle.Former IAS officer Ram Varma, who spent more than three decades in Haryana's administration and worked under all three of the state's famous political Lals, provides an insider's account of Devi Lal in his 2017 memoir 'Life in the IAS: My Encounters with the Three Lals of Haryana'.Varma describes Devi Lal as having the "aura of a kingmaker" and as a "leader of farmers", while portraying him as a warm and genial personality with an exceptionally strong mass following.Varma's description also places Devi Lal in the distinctive political tradition of Haryana's three Lals. In the book's foreword, he notes that Bansi Lal was the only one of the three to possess a university degree, while Devi Lal and Bhajan Lal acquired their political education through the "rough and tumble" of village-level politics. He records that Devi Lal had earlier served as parliamentary secretary under Punjab CM Partap Singh Kairon, giving him administrative experience before Haryana was created in 1966.That combination of grassroots politics and governmental experience helped turn Devi Lal into a formidable political operator.Devi Lal's influence had grown sharply by the late 1980s, when opposition parties were attempting to unite against Rajiv Gandhi's Congress.He became one of the principal forces behind the formation of the Janata Dal and helped bring disparate opposition groups into a common political platform. His enormous rural base in Haryana gave the anti-Congress coalition an organisational strength that leaders in Delhi could not easily ignore.His political stature was also on display in September 1989, when his 75th birthday became the occasion for a massive opposition rally in Delhi. VP Singh and several other opposition leaders attended, underlining the importance of Devi Lal in the emerging National Front coalition.Yet the relationship between the two men was more complicated than their public alliance suggested.VP Singh was the face of the anti-Rajiv Gandhi campaign at the national level, while Devi Lal possessed something Singh lacked: a formidable rural organisation and an established mass base in north India.By the time the election results were out, the question was no longer simply whether the opposition could form a government. It was who would control it.At around 7 pm on December 1, 1989, VP Singh met President R Venkataraman at Rashtrapati Bhavan with the documents establishing his election as leader of the National Front parliamentary party, along with letters of support from the BJP and Left parties. Venkataraman invited Singh to form the government and set December 2 for the swearing-in.The following day, VP Singh took oath as Prime Minister and Devi Lal took oath as deputy Prime Minister.But the political bargain did not bring lasting peace.The relationship between Singh and Devi Lal deteriorated rapidly as their competing political interests collided. Devi Lal became increasingly critical of the Prime Minister and emerged as the most powerful internal challenger to Singh.In August 1990, Singh removed Devi Lal from the Union cabinet. The following months saw the Janata Dal split, the BJP withdraw support and the VP Singh government fall.On November 9, 1990, Chandra Shekhar became Prime Minister with Devi Lal once again serving as deputy Prime Minister.Devi Lal's influence did not end with his death. It flowed into one of Haryana's most prominent political families.His son Om Parkash Chautala became one of Haryana's most consequential politicians and served as CM five times. Devi Lal's political legacy was subsequently carried through the Indian National Lok Dal, the party associated with the Chautala family.The next generation entered politics as well. Om Parkash Chautala's sons Ajay and Abhay Chautala became prominent leaders, while Ajay's sons Dushyant and Digvijay Chautala also entered electoral politics.But the family eventually split politically. Ajay Chautala and Dushyant Chautala broke away and formed the Jannayak Janta Party in 2018, while the INLD remained with Om Parkash Chautala and Abhay Chautala.The split fractured what had once been a formidable political inheritance. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, neither the INLD nor the JJP won a seat in Haryana, while the BJP and Congress won five seats each in the state.The contrast with Devi Lal's own era is striking. The man whose political clout once helped determine who would become India's Prime Minister left behind a family whose branches now operate through separate political formations.Devi Lal died in New Delhi on April 6, 2001, aged 86, after a political career that had taken him from the freedom movement and Haryana's villages to the centre of national coalition politics.
Article Summary: Chaudhary devi lal was the former haryana chief minister and deputy prime minister. He turned down the prime minister's post in 1989 in favour of vp singh. The episode, one of the more remarkable leadership reversals in political history, has been recounted in several accounts.

Article Title: EC faultlines have a long history, dating back to 1989
Article Text:
Election Commission of India

Poll Vote & Share your view Which internal conflict within the Election Commission do you find most concerning? NEW DELHI: It is not the first time that the fault lines within the Election Commission are out in the open. The trend started from the time it became a multi-member body in 1989.Two election commissioners S S Dhanoa and V S Seigell were appointed in October 1989 and joined the poll body then led by chief election commissioner (CEC) R V S Peri Sastri. Though Sastri never publicly spoke about it, it is widely believed that the new arrangement was perceived by him as a dilution in power. By January 1990, the appointment of the two commissioners was rescinded and the EC reverted to being a single—member body.In 1993, with T N Seshan as an all-powerful CEC, the commission was once again made a multi-member body with the appointment of election commissioners M S Gill and G V G Krishnamurthy. What followed was a running feud between Seshan on the one hand and Gill and Krishnamurthy on the other. Seshan viewed the appointments as a direct assault on the independence of his office and completely refused to recognize the two new commissioners. He refused to share official documents with Gill and Krishnamurthy, barred them from attending critical meetings, and would not allocate them any office work. He openly ridiculed the election commissioners in interviews, even referring to them as “two donkeys in my office”.Interestingly, it was on Seshan’s plea challenging the govt’s decision to make EC a multi-member body that the Supreme Court had, in 1995, ruled that the election commissioners and CEC were equal in status, power and decision-making authority and that the CEC was only “first among equals”.The other internal feud in EC to recall would be one between then CEC N Gopalaswami and election commissioner Navin Chawla between 2006 and 2009. Months before he was to step down upon the end of his tenure, Gopalaswami wrote to the President of India recommending the removal of Chawla on grounds of a pro-Congress bias. In his note to the President, Gopalaswami alleged that Chawla was passing on details of EC’s meetings to senior Congress leaders, often taking “toilet breaks” during commission meetings to do so. Gopalaswami’s recommendation was however turned down by the Manmohan Singh govt and Chawla succeeded him as CEC.During the 2019 general election, the differences between then CEC Sunil Arora and then election commissioner Ashok Lavasa came to the fore, with media reports alleging that he had dissented in cases relating to complaints of alleged model code of conduct violations by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and then BJP president Amit Shah, but was overruled without the commission making his dissent noted public. EC put out a clarification that dissent notes were only made public in quasi-judicial orders passed by EC.Lavasa resigned on August 18, 2020, two years short of his tenure, and joined the Manila-headquartered Asian Development Bank (ADB) as its Vice-President.Arun Goyal was the last election commissioner to quit in the middle of his term. Though he had cited personal reasons in his resignation dated March 9, 2024, it was widely speculated that he was not on the best of terms with the then chief election commissioner Rajiv Kumar.
Article Summary: The fault lines within the election commission are out in the open. The trend started from the time it became a multi-member body in 1989. Two election commissioners s s dhanoa and v s seigell were appointed in october 1989. By january 1990, the appointment of the two commissioners was rescinded and the ec reverted to being a single—member body.

‘Cannot talk about rigging selectively’

NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke has urged opposition parties to stop participating in elections if they believe the electoral process is being rigged, arguing that continued participation gives legitimacy to polls they themselves question.In a post on X on Friday, Dipke said opposition parties could not claim that elections were being rigged while continuing to contest them."Yes, elections are being rigged. But when you continue to participate in rigged elections, you legitimise these elections and help maintain the illusion that they are free and fair," he said.Dipke questioned whether opposition parties continued to contest elections because they feared losing their political presence if they stayed away."Maybe you keep contesting because you fear that if you don't, you will stop existing. But what kind of existence are you trying to protect when votes are being stolen, your MLAs and MPs are being poached, and your parties are being split?" he said."This is not political survival. You are simply trying to stay alive in a system that can weaken you, split your party or take away your elected representatives whenever it wants.How long can you survive like this?" Dipke asked.The CJP founder also accused opposition parties of raising allegations of election rigging selectively, depending on the state or political party involved."And you cannot talk about election rigging only when it happens in states that matter to you and remain silent when it happens elsewhere. If elections are being rigged, it should matter regardless of the state or which party is affected," the CJP convener said."You cannot keep saying the game is rigged while continuing to play it. Your participation is the only thing that gives these rigged elections legitimacy," he claimed.Dipke appealed to opposition parties to put democracy ahead of their political interests."Think about the nation and its democracy before thinking about your own political survival. Take a stand and stop participating in rigged elections."Dipke compared an allegedly manipulated election to a fixed cricket match, saying an election could still appear competitive even if its outcome had been predetermined."Just like in a fixed match, not every catch is dropped. Some catches are taken, and the match may even be dragged to the last over to make it look like a close fight," he said."In the same way, you will be handed a few wins, just enough to keep you contesting and to make people believe there was a real contest. Those few wins are the crumbs that keep you in the game and make the whole thing look legitimate," Dipke said.The remarks came a day after Dipke demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and threatened to launch a "Jantar Mantar 2.0" agitation if his demand was not met.They also followed a report by The Indian Express on Wednesday that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over the previous 10 months to decisions and orders of the Election Commission, including those concerning the addition, deletion and restoration of voters and changes to the voter registration process.Following the report, poll panel officials said the two commissioners had flagged decisions taken during voter-roll cleanup and the handling of the voter database in various states.EC sources maintained that all decisions of the Election Commission of India , including SIR, had been unanimous and approved by both election commissioners and the chief election commissioner.
Article Summary: Abhijeet dipke says opposition parties cannot claim elections are being rigged while continuing to contest them. The cjp founder compared an allegedly manipulated election to a fixed cricket match. He also accused opposition parties of raising allegations of election rigging selectively, depending on state or political party involved.
